title: Deep mutational scanning of H5 hemagglutinin to inform influenza virus surveillance
abstract: H5 influenza is considered a potential pandemic threat. Recently, H5 viruses belonging to clade 2.3.4.4b have caused large outbreaks in avian and multiple nonhuman mammalian species. Previous studies have identified molecular phenotypes of the viral hemagglutinin (HA) protein that contribute to pandemic potential in humans, including cell entry, receptor preference, HA stability, and reduced neutralization by polyclonal sera. However, prior experimental work has only measured how these phenotypes are affected by a handful of the >10,000 different possible amino-acid mutations to HA. Here, we use pseudovirus deep mutational scanning to measure how all mutations to a 2.3.4.4b H5 HA affect each phenotype. We identify mutations that allow HA to better bind α2-6-linked sialic acids and show that some viruses already carry mutations that stabilize HA. We also measure how all HA mutations affect neutralization by sera from mice and ferrets vaccinated against or infected with 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses. These antigenic maps enable rapid assessment of when new viral strains have acquired mutations that may create mismatches with candidate vaccine virus, and we show that a mutation present in some recent H5 HAs causes a large antigenic change. Overall, the systematic nature of deep mutational scanning combined with the safety of pseudoviruses enables comprehensive measurements of the phenotypic effects of mutations that can inform real-time interpretation of viral variation observed during surveillance of H5 influenza.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This PLoS Biology article has already shown unusually strong scholarly uptake for a 2024 publication, with 76 OpenAlex citations placing it in the top 1% of papers in its field and year. Its influence is especially visible in influenza and broader virology research, where it is being reused by both articles and preprints.

Full narrative

The study has been taken up quickly and broadly in the research literature. Of its 76 citations, 26 come from preprints, indicating early attention from active research communities, while the remainder are cited in published articles and a small number of reviews. The citing record is concentrated in influenza-focused work, but it also extends into respiratory virus research, animal disease epidemiology, and immune-response studies, suggesting that the paper is being used as a reference point beyond a single narrow subfield.

The downstream reuse pattern reinforces that impression. The article is documented as reused by 77 works overall, including 48 articles, 26 preprints, and 2 reviews. Several of the newer citing papers point directly to questions central to this study, such as H5 hemagglutinin binding, adaptation, thermostability, cleavability, and related molecular constraints on host range. That pattern suggests the paper is functioning as a methodological and conceptual resource for ongoing H5 influenza surveillance and risk-assessment research.

Public conversation around the paper is modest but present. Crossref event data records one news discussion item, and Bluesky shows one post engaging with the study’s deep mutational scanning findings and their implications for H5 phenotype. This is not a large public-facing footprint, but it does show that the paper has reached audiences outside formal citation channels.

The article’s research infrastructure is also well documented. It is gold open access, has linked data and code repositories, and is associated with multiple GitHub repositories and a Zenodo record. Funding support spans major biomedical and research organizations, including the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, NIAID/NIH, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and the National Institute of Health. Taken together, the record shows a paper with strong early scholarly influence, clear reuse in influenza-related research, and some limited but visible public discussion.
